WORKING ORGANIZATION. 


The following list of Committees shows how the working force of the 
Association, numbering about one hundred and fifty men, is organized. 
A list of the names of the Committeemen is published in a separate 
pamphlet, a copy of which may be obtained on application at the office. 


BUSINESS DEPARTMENT. 


Executive, Vacancies, Finance, Debt Fund, Membership. 


RELIGIOUS DEPARTMENT. 


A General Committee in charge of the whole Department and Special 
Committees, for the following items :—Young Men’s Meeting, Young Men’s 
Bible Study, Bible Study Courses, Sunday Morning Bible Class, Men’s 
Meeting, Hospital Work. 


SOCIAL DEPARTMENT. 


A General Committee for the Department and Special Committees 
for the Evening Reception work and the Strangers’ Tea. 


EDUCATIONAL DEPARTMENT. 


A General Committee in charge of the Evening Classes, Library and 
Reading-room. 


PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 


A General Committee for the Department, a corps of leaders who 
assist in conducting the Gymnasium Classes, and Special Committees on 
each of the following items of the department :—Cycling, Bowling, Hockey, 
Tennis, Basket Ball, Permanent Camp and Current Camp, Camera Club. 


JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


This Department has its own separate organization. Its work ts 
supervised by a General Executive Committee, composed of the Officers 
of the Department and seven members of the Senior Department of the’ 
Association. 


On 


Our Pressing Needs. 


———_+~<f op 


1. The balance of $20,000 required to complete the 
extinction of the Mortgage Debt on the Building. The 
Directors are pledged to pay this amount before December, 
1899. 


2. Seven thousand Dollars for the establishment of a 
Branch Building at Point St. Charles. The Grand Trunk 
Railway has promised $4,000 and a lot on condition that 
the Association provides the above-named amount,—the 
Building to be usedin common by the Railway employes 
and the other young men of that important section of the 
City. | 

3. An endowment Fund for the increase of our Library. 
We have 4,000 volumes, and we should have at least 
10,000. NoLibraryin the Cityisas largely used in propor- 
tion toits size. Because the wise direction of the reading 
of young men is so important a matter, we trust that some 
of our friends will respond to this appeal. 

4. An Endowment Fund for the supervision and ex- 
tension of the educational work of the Association. This 
is very important, as it most directly enables young men 
to help themselves.

The Forty-seventh Annual Meeting of the Association was held on 
Thursday evening, May 19th, at 8 o’clock, the President, Mr. H. B. Ames, 
in the chair. 


After devotional exercises the President called on Mr. 2). A. Budge, 
the Secretary, to read his Annual Report. Reports of Committees were 
also presented as follows :—

On motion of Mr. L. H. Packard, seconded by Mr. A. W. Payne, the 
reports, as read, were adopted and ordered to be published for circulation 
among the members and subscribers. 


The following notice of motion, as presented at the previous Annual 
Meeting, was read :— 


Resolved: That the following clause be added to Section 4 of 
Article I of the By-Laws of the Association: “Any member who, after 
the passing of this amendment, pays the Full Membership Fee for twelve 
consecutive years (and always renews his membership within one mouth 
of its expiration), shall be entitled to full privileges for life, provided that 
no cause arises which would render him ineligible to admission as a 
member.” 


On motion of Mr. C. W. Brown, seconded by Mr. Wm. Drysdale, 
this amendment was adopted. 


The following gentlemen were nominated as Directors for the three 
years ending May Ist, 1901 :—Messrs. 1). W. Ross, Chas. T. Williams, 
J. W. Knox, D. Bentley, H. B. Ames, G. H. Harrower and C. E. Gault. 
No other nominations being offered, these gentlemen were unanimously 
elected. 


A resolution of thanks to the city press for gratuitous notices, etc., 
was carried, and it was ordered that a telegram be sent to Mr. T. Duncan 
Patton, Secretary of the Winnipeg Association, congratulating him on the 
inauguration of their Building movement. 


The meeting adjourned after devotional exercises. 


Forty-Seventh Annual Report. 


This building for Montreal’s 
young men has stood with its 
doors open daily during the past 
year from 7 A. M. until 10 P.M. 
as an expression of the religion of 
Jesus Christ and the intelligent 
and unselfish interest felt by the 
business men and citizens of this 
community in its young men. 
‘“A City’s greatest asset is its young 
men.” The Young Men’s Chris- 
tian Association enters the field 
in order to reach and save these 
young men and better equip them 


to fill their places as business men and citizens. 


The history of the Association shows that it has wisely adapted itself to 
the needs of the various classes of young men. While thus keeping 
abreast of the times we must never lose sight of the fact that the power 
and permanent usefulness of the Association does not depend upon the 
greatness of its numbers or the variety of its work, but upon its adherence 
to this foundation principle, viz: that each member should seek by direct 
and indirect effort in the sphere of his daily calling to bring his fellow 
young men under helpful christian influences, and, in the end, to a loyal 
surrender of their lives to the Saviour of the world. 


In entering on the forty-eighth year of the work we would emphasize this 
fir-t principle which called the parent Association into existence in 1844, 
and urge each of our active members to use his influence with the young 
men of his own acquaintance with whom he works and spends his leisure 
hours, and we must ever judge of the success and usefulness of the Asso- 
ciation by this standard. 


8 


The reports to be presented will show how the work in the following 
departments has been prosecuted :—Finance, Membership, Building Fund, 
Religious, Social and Reception, Educational, Physical, Junior, Sumnier 
Camp, Reading Room and Library, Hospital, Employment, Foreign Work, 
&c. This amount of work has only been possible through the large 
volunteer force of men on the various committees who have so cheerfully 
devoted their time and effort to this end. The Directors take this oppor- 
tunity of thanking these committee-men for their valuable assistance. 


Appended to this report will be found a statistical summary of the year’s 
work. Statistics, however, cannot serve as a substitute for personal contact 
and observation. The influence for righteousness, which has been of a 
personal nature, cannot easily be recorded. Eternity will show that the 
largest part of this good work has been accomplished through the individual 
efforts of the members and their intercourse with the young men in the 
Association building. 


The Property. At the beginning ofthe year the Directors faced the 
loss of a tenant occupying the larger part of two floors in the building. 
This made our position very serious. But, in answer to prayer, what was 
a great loss has already begun to turn out for the best. The financial 
difficulty thus involved led one cf our members, Mr. Alex. Arthur, to 
propose that a Committee of the young men, acting independently of the 
Directors, should secure one hundred men from among the members who 
would endeavor to raise $100 each before November, 1899, toward the 
extinction of the mortgage debt of $50,000 on the building. ‘Their report 
will speak for itself. It was the statement of their voluntary action in the 
Board meeting last November which decided the Directors to make the 
attempt to clear off the whole indebtedness. At the present time $28,000 
has been subscribed toward the amount being raised by the Board of 
Directors, and it is hoped that this canvass may be continued and com- 
pleted during the year. The first payment of $10,000 on the reduction of 
the mortgage debt will be made on June lst. Thus what seemed to be a 
most serious problem will turn out for the best interest of the Association. 


Third and Fourth Floors. The Directors decided to alter the 
fourth floor and part of the third floor so as to provide rooms for members, 
thus devoting the building entirely to the purpose for which it was erected. 
On February first the changes on the fourth floor were completed and all 
the roons on that floor are now occupied. On June first the changes on 


9 


the third floor will be completed. Altogether this will give accommodation 
for thirty-seven young men and also provide a set of four splendid class- 
rooms for the Educational Department. ‘The cost of these improvements 
and furnishings will be about $6500. The revenue to be derived from 
these floors will justify the expenditure, besides making the fullest and most 
satisfactory use of the property of the Association. 


Finatice. It is essential to the success of an Association that its 
financial affairs should be carefully administered. Such has been the 
Finance Committee’s aim this year. In view of the shrinkage in revenue 
the work of the Association was necessarily curtailed. In this connection 
the Directors cannot speak too highly of the arduous and self-denying 
efforts of the Finance Committee, which make it possible in the face of 
such difficulties to close the year with all bills paid for current expenses. 
This result was only attained through the generous action of several of our 
Directors. For this we would express our gratitude to God, as well as for 
his never-failing care through all these years. 


The Staff. The Association sustained a great loss through the resig- 
nation, owing to ill-health, of Mr. W. F. Chapman in June last. We are 
glad to know that the year spent in rest and out-door work has caused a 
hopeful improvement. His place was filled by Mr. Archie Mackellar, one 
of the workers who came up through the Physical Department. Mr. A'ex. 
R. Ross succeeded Mr. Ellerbeck in charge of the Library. 


Bequests. On March 24th we received $1800 from the Executors 
of the estate of the late Robert Anderson. We arealso nctified that $500 
has been bequeathed to the Association by the late W J. Withall, and will 
be payable this year. By the will of the late W. B. Hamilton $1000 was 
bequeathed to the Association but has not yet been paid. May we suggest 
to those who have the best interests of young men at heart that in following 
these examples they may provide a fund which will be speaking in w trie 
and deeds of kindness through future years. 


Railway Bratch. The work for Railway Men at Point St. Charles 
has been affiliated with the Association and will be reported upon to-night. 
A promising work has been carried on throughout the year with a Sec- 
retary in charge during the evenings. This, we hope, will soon develop 
into a broad work, with extended privileges, including the young men in 
that important section of the city. 


10 


D.L. Moody. Through its Religious Work Committee the Asso- 
ciation secured two visits during the year from Mr. D. L. Moody, and during 
his visits daily meetings were held in St. James Methodist Church which 
were of the greatest benefit to the spiritual life of the city. The Association 
also planned Mr. Moody’s tour through the important towns and cities of 
Ontario and Manitoba. 


The Bible Class Work for the past year has been a most encour- 
aging feature, five classes having been held each week with excellent 
results. It is only as the Word of God is kept in the fore-front that men 
will be developed so as to take a permanent, unselfish and unflagging in- 
terest in the highest welfare of their fellows. 


In addition to the regular religious meetings of the Association an added 
gathering has been held on Sunday evenings after the church services. 
This Song Service has become popular, and will fill an important place in 
the Sunday evening life of many members and others. It is largely attended 
by those who room in the building. . 


Suimmer Camp. The Permanent Camp Committee has made prog- 
ress in securing additional islands in Lac St. Joseph, Ste. Agathe, and 
adding a building so that members can have the option of living in tents 
or buildings. The Camp promises to prove more popular than ever. 


Foreign Work. The Association members still continue their interest 
in the less favored young men of India. The most encouraging reports 
come from our representative in India, Mr. David McConaughy, and the 
building at Madras is now completed. We are greatly favored in having 
the opportunity of co-operating through such a consecrated and able rep- 
resentative. ‘Iwo of our members have, during the past year, gone to the 
foreign field: Dr. Percy C. Leslie to China, on behalf of the Canadian 
Presbyterian Board, and Mr. Kristen Borup to Africa, under the direction 
of the Church Missionary Society. We regret to learn that Rev. Thos. H. 
Allan, who went to” Africa, has fallen a victim to fever. We hope that 
each year may see some of our members offering themselves for the foreign 


field. 
Outlook for Next Year. New Developments. 


1. We need a young man who can give his entire time to the Functor 
Department. Some of the best and most promising workers in our Asso- 
ciation to-day have come from the Juniorranks. The peculiar nature and 


1] 


importance of their work demands better supervision than in the past. 
We will ask the Finance Committee for a suitable man for at least nine 
months of the year. 


2. We will ask for a special committee to develop our present Bible 
work on more thorough and comprehensive lines, say the establishment of 
a “Lay- Workers’ Bible Institute” for the training of Sunday-School Teach- 
ers and lay christian workers, and affording them an Opportunity for a more 
thorough and systematic study of the Bible. Such an institute would be 
exceedingly helpful to churches and Sunday-Schools, and to other depart- 
ments of philanthropic and religious work. With the facilities afforded in 
our building we hope to see this inaugurated next fall. 


3. Better Social Work. We have not succeeded in making the 
best use of the social opportunities afforded by this building. We hope 
to place this matter in the hands of a wise committee whom we will ask 
to work it out on broader lines. 


4. An Association Paper. ‘he financial difficulty was the chief 
reason for suspending the issue of the “Association Record” last year. 
This must not occur another year. Our inability to keep members and 
subscribers fully informed as to the work of the building was a great loss. 
We will ask for an appropriation to meet this expense and a special Com- 
mittee to take charge of the issue of the paper, so as to relieve the office as 
far as possible. 

5. Athletic Grounds. We need the use of recreation grounds for 
our summer work. If this could be secured, with a water front where 
swimming and boating privileges could be had, it would be a great addition 
to the membership privileges. 


We deeply regret having to record the death of the following subscribers 
and members during the year :— 


F. W. FaiRMAN, a member since 1874. Da. R. C. KIRKPATRICK, 


L.. H PIGNOLET, 1 Ds LO

FINANCE. 


Continuous and careful supervision has been given to the financial affairs of the 
Association. At the beginning of the year the ‘‘ estimates” were cut in each department 
so as to effect a saving of $1168.00 over last year’s expenditure. This was rendered 
necessary in view of the reduction in revenue from rental of $2500.00. The following 
estimates were made for the Committee’s guidance :—

The amount expended for alterations and equipments on the third and fourth floors 
will be about $6,000. This is not included in the financial statement submitted, but is 
carried as a special fund. which it is hoped to reduce annually on the completion of these 


alterations. It is expected that the Association will have an earning power from rentals 
equal to its former revenue. 


Through the generosity of our regular subscribers, and the special subscriptions of 
several Directors and friends, this year has been closed as usual with all bills paid. 


H. J. MUDGE, 


Chairman.

MEMBERSHIP. 


Last year a Membership Contest was held, which resulted in the addition of over six 
hundred members. This was phenomenal. The Committee deemed it unwise to hold 
a similar contest this year. The appointment of the Debt Fund Committee in No- 
vember last took some of the best membership workers from this Committee. These 
facts in part account for the shrinkage in members as reported. 


469 new members joined during the year. The detailed statement is as follows :— 


No. Fees. 
VAIS ,. o5 bea ms nak pO a 157 $434. 
DSFAEE o. ors go. Ga whe Eek 278 
Pete ate orn asisieg aA OR ARS 962 
PSEA 5G 5s ae ke ao inten. ee 5,675.42 
— 1,467 
Sle BIE SEONOIBIY sok 5d 6 lace as 23 
PMR, ho tak wank ¢ ak Coes wei 94 
HORE T TS x si od cee a eae 112 
POUR 2 eer, Sy ee 1,696 
Active. Associate. 
616 694 


It seems a small request to ask that each member interests himself to secure one or 
more new members. Many do it now. But if one-half our members would respond the 
usefulness of the Association could be increased tenfold. Some suggestions to note and 
follow :— 

1. Send or leave your name and address of a prospective niember at the office. 

2. Invite young men who come as strangers to the city to visit the Building. Make 
an appointment to meet them. Introduce them at the office. 

3. Name a list of the young men in your church, or among your acquaintance, and 
leave it at the office. Printed matter will be sent andthe Committee will make personal 
canvass. 

4, Be frank to make suggestions concerning the present plans and possible develop- 
ment of the work. This will be welcomed by and carefully considered by the Committee. 


C. W. BROWN, 


Chairniai.

YOUNG MEN’S DEBT FUND. 


In November last the idea was conceived that the debt of over $50,000 remaining 
on our building should be wiped out and that the young men should undertake $10,000 
of the amount, to be raised by getting one hundred of our active members to collect one 
hundred dollars each within two years. With this object in view a meeting was at once 
called which appointed a committee to select a Chairman, Treasurer and Secretary. 
These officers, together with two auditors, were appointed, and a committee of ten was 
formed to take charge of the undertaking. One hundred collecting books were secured 
and the canvass started. We have much pleasure in stating that all of the books have 
been placed and $2,725 pledged. This has meant a large amount of work for the com- 
mittee, which has met every Tuesday evening since its formation for prayer and conference. 


We wish to thank all who have assisted in the effort and solicit the co-operation and 
sympathy of all our members in this work. Much remains to be done before we get the 
amount which the Committee is determined to raise within the time mentioned or earlier 


if possible. 
We believe that we have so far had the help and guidance of our Heavenly Father, 
and are assured that we shall have it till this work is accomplished. 


ALEX. ARTHUR, 


Chatrnian. 


READING ROOM and LIBRARY. 


The Reading Room tables are furnished with 153 papers and magazines. This list 
contains Daily, Weekly, Monthly, Quarterly publications. 108 of these are purchased at 
a cost of $245.05, and 45 are donated by the publishers. We are pleased to notice an 
increasing attendance of members who regularly use this important educational bureau. 

The use of the Reading Room by strangers and non-members is also increasing 


each year. : 

We would suggest to the new Committee the 
advisability of securing duplicate copies of some 
of the leading magazines and placing them on 
the tables in the Parlors for the use of members 
only. This would increase the use of the Parlors 
by the members and relieve the pressure on 
the Reading Room. 


The Library has been very largely used 
in proportion to the number of volumes on 
the shelves. 6,590 books have been drawn 
by 793 different members.

45 by gift; the names and donors are here 
added. We trust our members will keep the 
Association Library in their mind for donation

this opportunity and continued the work throughout the six months. The total enrol-

BIBLE STUDY COURSES. 


Tuesday evenings from October to April were set apart for special courses of Bible 
study, and three successful classes were held ; Mr. Budge conducted one class, studying 
the Gospel of St. John; Mr. Calhoun conducted another, studying an outline of the Old 
Testament, and Mr. Ball conducted a third class, studying the life of Christ. The total 
average attendance at these classes was 35. 


On Sunday morning at 9.45 a class was also held for beginners in Bible study, con- 
ducted by Mr. Calhoun, which had an average attendance of about 18. 


The results of these courses of study have been very satisfactory; several of the 
members have expressed their sense of the value of these classes in promoting the more 
thorough and systematic study of the Bible. 


The Committee would suggest that this work be continued next season on even 
broader and more comprehensive lines. The men who are interested in Bible study on 
these special lines ought to look forward by united action to the formation of a Bible 
study club, or organization of some kind that would plan for the conduct of each year’s 
work. Still greater results would be attained. 

A. ARTHUR, 
Chazirniai. 


HOSPITAL WORK. 


The work of visitation in the various Hospitals has been continued with much profit 
throughout the year. A Sunday morning service for the patients has been held each 
week in the wards of the Western Hospital, and has, we have great reason to believe, 
been a means of blessing to many. We have also held a Sunday afternoon service in the 
Homwepathic Hospital each week, from April to October, while the Theological Colleges 
are closed. 

The Sunday morning service in the chapel at the General Hospital has been discon- 
tinued on account of the difficulty experienced in getting any considerable number of the 
patients to attend at that hour. The distance of the chapel from the wards also deterred 
many of the patients from attending. 


N. V. McLEOD, 


Chairmai. 


aa 


YOUNG MEN’S MEETING. 


Meetings have been held every Saturday evening during the year, with the exception 
of Christmas, when an appropriate morning service was substituted, and on New Year's 
the regular meeting being postponed on account of the Annual Reception on that day. 
The meetings have been well attended throughout the entire year, the average attendance 
being 63. A pleasing feature of the meeting has been the attendance of a number of men 
from outside the city. 

From the many bright and cheerful testimonies heard at our meetings, we believe 
mea are being helped and encouraged in the christian life. ; 

The Committee are deeply indebted to Mr. Ball for his valuable assistance in leading 
the singing, but we feel the need of a number of young men to assist him, and thus make 


the meetings more bright and helpful. 
LEWIS A. WINTER, 


Chairman. 
YOUNG MEN’S BIBLE CLASS. 


Your Committee have much pleasure in submitting the following report for the year 
just closed :— ) 

The attendance at the class for the season was 3988, an average of 77 per Sunday ; 
the largest attendance being on January 9th—120; and the smallest on June 20th — 40. 

During the Summer months we followed a short course of topical studies, and in the 
Fall started a biographical course on the lives of the three great apostles —Peter, John, 
and Paul —which have been very helpful and interesting, the blackboard and map having 
been used through the course. 

On January 9th the Annual Class Tea was held, at which there were about 130 
present, including a number of the older members who had gone out from the Class to 
other branches of christian work, and who gave splendid testimonies of the training they 
received while in the Class. The Tea was one of the most successful ever held. One of 
the pleasant features was the presentation of a handsome writing desk to Mr. Woods 
Walmsley, who has so faithfully performed the duty of Organist for the Class for so 
miany years. . ; 

Through our monthly collection we have been able to defray the expense of printing 
and other items, and to send a delegate from the Class to the Inter-Provincial Convention 
held at Brantford in January. / 

We desire to thank the following gentlemen who have led the Class during Mr. 
Budge’s absence— Mr. John Currie, Rev. E. Scott, Mr. C. K. Calhoun and Mr. W, H. Ball. 
We also had the pleasure of having Mr. Webster, one of the Keswick Brethren, lead us 
for one Sunday, which was greatly enjoyed. 

A. MACKELLAR, 
Chairman. 


SOCIAL WORK. 


The Social Committee had charge of the arrangements for the Annual Socials in the 


Building this year as in former years. These comprised :— 


1. The Opening Fall Reception on October 5th, when a very fine musical programme 
was given through the kindness of Mr. Ernest Kerr, Organist, and the Choir of Olivet 
Baptist Church. Refreshments were served through the kind provision of the ladies of 
St Gabriel, Sherbrooke Street and Chalmer’s Churches. 


2. An informal reception to new members on the evening of November 5th, when an 


enjoyable programme was given and refreshments served at the close. 


3. The New Year's Reception on New Year’s afternoon and evening. The Building 
was tastefully decorated for the occasion. A series of events was arranged in the 
Gymnasium, but the chief interest centred in the Basket Ball Match between the Business 
Men and the Office Staff. The evening programme in the Association Hall was 
thoroughly enjoyed. Our hearty thanks are due to the ladies who so kindly looked after 


the refreshments in the afternoon. 


4. The Closing Reception was held on Tuesday evening, April 19th, when a very 
pleasant evening was spent by a large number of the members and their friends. The 
ladies of St. Paul’s, Dominion Square, and Crescent Street Churches, provided the 


refreshments, and have our hearty thanks. 


The Committee would like to express its sense of obligation to all the friends whose 
kind assistance on the various programmes and otherwise contributed to the pleasure and 


success of these social occasions. 


C. K. CALHOUN, 


for the Commitice, 


to 
ti | 


STRANGERS TEA. 


Your Committee wish to report that five Strangers’ teas were held during the year, 
in the months of September, October, November, December and February. All young 
men, of whose recent arrival in the city the Association had learned, were invited. The 
teas were usually held on the first Sunday evening of the month at 5.15 p.m., and were 
presided over by different members of the Board of Directors. After tea each young man 
present introduced himself, and this enabled every one present to get acquainted. A 
pleasant hour was then spent in singing, and the occasion was brought to a close by the 
reading of a passage of Scripture and prayer. The young men present were very ready 
in expressing their appreciation of the kindness shown them, and we believe that many of 
them have been helped and that all have been led to see the benefit of the Association, 
especially to a young man coming as a stranger to the city. 

GEO: J. COMRIE, 


Chairman. 


EVENING RECEPTION. 


The evening reception work has been carried on throughout the year and the com- 
mittee has endeavored to keep at least one man on duty each evening to welcome 
strangers, show them through the building and take an interest in their welare. 
Considerable difficulty has been found in obtaining workers for this committee, which is 
very much to be regretted, as it affords one of the most pleasant and useful spheres of work 
within the reach of the Association. It is to be hoped that during this year upon which 
we are entering we shall see many of the older workers in the Association taking active 
work on this committee. Our building has a bright appearance on the outside, but unless 
we can extend an open hand and make it bright inside by our workers taking a personal 
interest in the hundreds of young men that visit it every evening, it will largely fail in 
its object. 

Ww. A. GANDLE, 
Chairman. 


EMPLOYMENT. 


Applications for employment were fyled with us by 520 young men. Seventy of 
these obtained situations through the Association, and many others were assisted in their 
efforts in this direction.

PHYSICAL DEPARTMENT. 


Comparing the work with previous years, we have to repeat that while in some 
branches the interest has diminished, in others there has been a marked increase. Amongst 
the former may be mentioned the Bowling Club, Snow-shoe Club. and from lack of 
suitable grounds the Lacrosse, Football and Base-bal]l Clubs, while in the Tennis Club, 
Hockey Club, and the Summer Camp at Lake St. Joseph, great activity has been 
manifested. 


BASKET BALL.—Basket Ball has been popular as ever. A Tournament of five teams, 
composed of 47 players, was formed and won by the ‘* Stars,” with a record of seven 
games won and one lost, and the closeness of the contest is shown by the fact that three 
teams tied for second place. Exhibition Games were played on New Year's Day, and 
on the evening of the closing Reception. Tournaments were also formed amongst Juniors 
with twenty-five players, and amongst the boys with sixty-five players. 


TENNIS CLuB.—The Tennis Club adopted the challenge system for the ranking. of 
players with a great deal of interest, and a tournament was commenced but not completed 
at the close of the season. The lot adjoining the building will be in good shape for 
Tennis, and we hope to see a large number of members playing the game. 


LEADERS’ CLAsSs.—The Leaders’ Class is composed of sixteen members, who meet 
each week under Mr. Ball’s direction for practice. They also make a study of physiology, 
assist in the examinations, and act as judges for the graded examinations and of the cham- 
pionship contests. There is also a leaders’ class of ten school boys and five junior leaders. 


HockEy CLus.—The Hockey Club has sixty members, who have evinced a lively 
interest in the game. The Crystal Rink was hired for each Monday evening from ten to 
eleven o'clock, and Thursday evenings from 6.45 to 7.45 ; alternate nights were used for 
practices and for the Tournament matches. The Tournament between four teams playing 
twelve matches, ended in a tie for both first and second places, the final matches not 
being played: off owing to the close of the season. The finances show a balance on hand 
of $13 50. 


27 


GYMNASIUM WorRK.—The attendance at the classes has been somewhat smaller 
than usual, due partly to the smaller number of new members joining the Association last 
year, and the exceptionally fine Fall, Winter and early Spring, which attracted the mem- 
bers to outdoor exercise. We hope that more of our members will appreciate the 
value of systematic exercise, which may be carried on under such careful supervision and 
advice as is given by our Physical Director.

The Championships of the Association were won as follows :— 
Swimming, H. Sharpe, 438 points. 
Athletics, (Pentathlon) L. Cushing, 355 poinis. 
Gymnastics, A. E. Smaill, 82% 
All-Round Champion, A. E. Smaill, 720 out of a possible 1100. 


SNow-SHOE CLUB.—The Snow-Shoe Club reports a very poor season owing to lack 
of interest in the sport. A number of tramps were held with very small attendance. 


BOWLING CLUB.—The Bowling Club report only a fair season. The finances are 
in excellent condition, leaving a balance of $16.98. No tournament or matches with 
outside clubs were held. The Club record with much regret the death of their Honorary 
President, R. C. Kirkpatrick, M.D. 


PERMANENT CAMP COMMITTEE.—This Committee has charge of the property of 
the Summer Camp at Lake St. Joseph. Two islands of those under lease have been 
purchased from the Government, and a substantial log kitchen and ice-house have been 
built thereon at a cost of $75.00. Blankets and tents have been purchased at a cost of 
about one hundred dollars. The fishing rights of the adjoining Lake St. Mary have been 
leased for ten years. During the Fall and Winter, plans were made for the erection of a 
log cabin 40 x 22 feet, with a large open fire-place. The contracts were let this Spring 
for the sum of $450.00, and active canvas has been made among the members, directors, 
and friends of those interested in the Camp, and $350 has been subscribed. The outlook 
for the coming season is very bright. With a permanent and comfortable residence in 
addition to the tents, with good fishing, and improved transportation, it is scarcely pos- 
sible to find a more desirable Summer resort for young men. 


CuRRENT CAMP COMMITTEE.— This Committee is appointed by the Permanent 
Camp Committee each season to take charge of the Summer Camp. Last year 48 different 
men attended the Camp during the Summer season, the average length of stay being 


28 


fourteen days. Finances show expenses $593.53, receipts $628.77, leaving a balance on 
hand of $35.24. In addition to the regular Summer Camp, two different parties used 
the Camp, the first on the Queen’s Birthday and the second for ten days in September. 
These parties numbered seven and eight members. Junior Camp was held during the 
first two weeks in July with an attendance of 24. During the winter, several reunions 
and receptions have been held by the Campers. 


GYMNASTIC EXHIBITIONS.—The Exhibition arranged for by last year’s Committee, 
and which was held during the month of May, 1897, in the Windsor Hall, was a success- 
ful entertainment, although the receipts did not cover the expenditure. 


Fretp Day.—Field Day was held on the M.A.A.A. Grounds on Thursday, 23rd 
day of September, and was more successful than the previous year The finances show 
a surplus of some $30.00. The Committee has, this year, determined to hold it if pos- 


sible on a Saturday afternoon in September, and an application has been made for the 
use of the M.A.A.A. grounds. 


The number of physical examinations made have been 291 Seniors and 85 Juniors, 
Doctors W. H. Drummond, D. J. Evans, and W. F. Hamilton rendering efficient and 
much valued assistance. 


We would respectfully call the attention of the Directors to the urgent need of having 
the promised examination rooms in order for the use of the Doctors next September, and 
that the floor of the Gymnasium be put into proper condition. Some method of venti- 
lating the Locker-Rooms and Gymnasium is urgently needed. 

JOHN W. ROSS, 
Chairman.

JUNIOR DEPARTMENT. 


The work of the Junior Department has been carried on very satisfactorily during 
the past year, considering the heavy drafts that have been made upon the time of the 
Secretary. The Committee feel very strongly that, in order to accomplish good results, 
the Department requires the full time ofa Junior Secretary. This is a strategic point in 
the work of the Association, and it is manifestly impossible to carry it to any successful 
issue, when the Secretary is only allowed to spend a limited portion of his time in con- 
nection with it. The committee fully appreciate the difficulties under which the Asso- 
ciation labours, and the heavy stress of work at certain times of the year, but feel very 
keenly the fact that at the most critical periods of the year, in the fall. the holiday season, 
and the early spring, the time of the Junior Secretary is entirely taken up with Senior 
work. In this way the most valuable opportunities are lost, as the Secretary is the one 
who comes most into contact with the boys and forms the connecting link between them 
and the Association. 


The membership shows a falling off as compared with last year, due partly to the 
fact that many who joined at the time of the membership contest, failed to renew. The 
present membership is 157, as compared with 210 at the corresponding time last year, 
and is made up as follows :— | 


uae ls oe CEN es He ee as 65 
ees aeRO E SC or an ek Wala eae ee OS 92 


Seventeen members renewed in the Seniors. 


The Friday night meeting has been held regularly as_ usual, with an average attend- 
ance of 35 during the season, and 8 during July and August. In addition to this a train- 
ing class has been held on Sunday afternoons at 4.30, with an average attendance of 6. 
A service of song has béen held by the boys on the first Sunday of each month, at the 
General Hospital, with special services at Christmas and Easter. In this connection, we 
would suggest that a boys’ Glee-club be added to the Educational work next year, with a 
competent instructor, as we feel that it would prove of great value to the boys and would 
be greatly appreciated. 


The Library this year was thoroughly overhauled, and a new partition put up around 
it, which has enabled us to keep the books in much better shape. 115 new books were 
added, and as evidence of the interest taken in this branch of the work, it may be men- 
tioned that since Jan. 21st, 620 books have been taken out by 99 different readers, or an 
average of about 6 books per reader for 3 months. There are now 694 books in the 
library, representing about 40 authors, and 14 magazines on file in the reading-room. 


The social events have comprised an opening social on Nov. 4th, when the enter- 
tainment and refreshments were provided by the young people of Erskine Church, a lime- 
light lecture on the ‘‘Honey bee and his relations”, on Dec. 6th, by Mr. C. T. Williams, 
and the annual spring social on 28th April, all of which were well attended and proved — 
very enjoyable. 


The Summer Camp has now become one of the recognized features of the work and 
last year proved as popular as ever. The Secretary and 24 boys were out for two weeks 
from June 25th to July 9th, and it not only makes a capital holiday, but creates a very 


30 


pleasant social feeling between the boys who go. A reunion of the Campers was held on 
Jan. 10th, when an excellent menu was discussed and a Camp-fire held in the game-room. 


The interest in the Athletic work has been well sustained and the classes held reg- 
ularly, with an average attendance of 43 in the School-boy’s classes and of 28 in the even- 
ing classes for the working-boys. 

The most notable event in the past season, however, was the reorganization of the 
Department on somewhat different lines from those in use heretofore. The Executive 
Committee felt that the boys would take greater interest in the work if allowed to elect 
their own officers and committees among themselves. The question was very carefully 
considered, and finally a meeting of the members was called and the plan fully explained 
to them. It proved very popular, and at an adjourned meeting the officers and chairmen 
of the various committees were elected, and the boys themselves now conduct the business 
of the Department, subject to the approval of the Executive Committee, who still control 
the work and are represented on the various committees. 


The plan has only been in operation a couple of months but gives every evidence of 
being a success, and the Committee hopes that it will not only interest the boys, but prove 
of value to them as a training in business methods and committee work. A post-card 
monthly is now issued giving all the notices and items of interest in connection with the 
Department. 

WE. CUSHING, 


Chatrvinan.
